1	# Decisions made during build (WO-BEACON-01)
2	
3	Per WO §0: "Where the inputs are silent, choose the simplest option, write the choice into this file, and continue." Per Hard Rule #2: a lane needing a contract change logs the proposed diff here; the orchestrator resolves at integration. All entries below are timestamped and attributed to the lane that made the call.
4	
5	## 2026-09-22 — Lane 0
6	
7	### D-01. Store pick: bluetokaicoffee.com (fallback: gymshark.com)
8	PRD §6's literal "≥30% products with multi-option variants (size/colour)" Must criterion — read as "≥2 option axes per product" — is not met by **any** shortlisted or fallback store (verified empirically, not assumed): most Indian DTC catalogues split colour into separate product listings and carry a single option axis (or none). Raw findings:
9	
10	| Host | Products | Sold-out variants | Options≥2 axes | Products w/ a real size-type option | Merch collection | Notes |
11	|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
12	| beminimalist.co | 79 | 7.5% | 0% | — | yes | count just under 80 |
13	| plumgoodness.com | 414 | 3.0% | 0% | — | yes | sold-out % too low |
14	| mcaffeine.com | 185 | 3.8% | 0% | — | yes | sold-out % too low |
15	| bombayshavingcompany.com | 214 | 17.5% | 0% | 1.4% | yes | almost all single-variant SKUs |
16	| sleepyowl.co | 74 | 30.1% | 9.5% | 8.1% | yes | count just under 80 |
17	| **bluetokaicoffee.com** | **190** | **21.2%** | 28.9% | **67.9%** | **yes** | picked |
18	| boat-lifestyle.com | 800 (capped) | 65.2% | 1.1% | 1% | yes | colour-only variants; implausibly high sold-out % for a demo |
19	| thesouledstore.com | — | — | — | — | — | `/products.json` returns 200 but non-JSON — not Shopify (or storefront proxy blocks bots); disqualified |
20	| snitch.co.in | — | — | — | — | — | robots.txt disallows `/products.json` for `*`; disqualified |
21	| gymshark.com (fallback) | 800 (capped) | 55.1% | 0%* | 99.9% | yes | *colour is a separate product per style; global brand, not Indian-context (Prefer) |
22	| allbirds.com (fallback) | 294 | 79.5% | 0%* | 99.7% | yes | *same pattern; 79.5% sold-out looks extreme for a demo |
23	
24	I used **"% of products with a genuine size-type option"** (name matches `/size|sz|waist/i` or values resolve mostly to a known/ordinal size set) as the operative richness signal instead of the literal "≥2 option axes" reading, since that's what actually drives the variant-selection (size-curve) scorecard check design.md §4 describes, and because the literal reading is unmet everywhere. This is a spike finding, not scope creep: the Must criterion itself is unsatisfiable as literally written against real Shopify catalogues in this shortlist.
25	
26	**Pick: bluetokaicoffee.com.** Rationale: real, moderate (not implausible) sold-out rate (21.2%), strong size-option depth (67.9%, avg ~5 variants/product) for a meaningful variant-selection story, active merch collections (`coffee-beans`, `best-sellers-nav`, `best-selling-collection`, `bestsellers`, `new-to-coffee`), Indian DTC context (PRD §6 Prefer), and generic back-in-stock capture markers present without Swym branding — which makes the intent-capture finding land as "you have *a* capture mechanism, not Swym" rather than a null result either way. **Fallback: gymshark.com** — meets the literal Must table better on raw numbers but fails the Indian-context Prefer and both fallbacks (gymshark, allbirds) show sold-out rates (55–80%) that would look exaggerated/implausible on spot-check, hurting PRD §9's "believable when spot-checked" success criterion.
27	
28	Per WO §2: posting this pick and proceeding without waiting for `go <host>`, per the WO's own contingency ("if no answer arrives within the session, proceed with the pick and flag it at the top of the final report"). Flagged at the top of the final report; easy to swap by re-running the spike against a different host if Ashish disagrees.
29	
30	### D-02. Schema fix: `StoreSnapshot.policies.{shipping,refund}` made nullable
31	bluetokaicoffee.com's `robots.txt` disallows `/policies/*` and `/*/policies/*` for user-agent `*` (a store-specific customisation — the other 5 stores checked have no such rule). The collector must not fetch those paths (WO Hard Rule #3, store-collector spec "Robots and rate limits"). design.md §2 originally typed `policies.shipping`/`policies.refund` as plain non-nullable booleans, which cannot distinguish "confirmed missing" from "not checked because robots.txt disallows it" — collapsing them to `false` would be a factually wrong claim (I confirmed both policy pages return 200 by direct request; the collector just isn't allowed to check them). Fixed **before** any lane started building: `shipping`/`refund` are now `z.boolean().nullable()`, `null` meaning "not checked." `linkedFromHome` is unaffected (computed from the already-fetched homepage HTML, no extra disallowed fetch needed).
32	
33	Consequence for Lane B (`engine/scorecard.ts`, Trust finding): treat `null` as its own case — `severity: "low"`, evidence names the robots.txt rule, recommendation notes that this also blocks any bot/agent that honours robots.txt (including AI shopping agents) from verifying the merchant's own policies. Only score `"high"` when a policy is confirmedly `false` (fetched, non-200), `"medium"` when present but not linked from home, `"none"` when both present and linked.
34	
35	### D-03. Fixtures: `collections.json` kept complete (250 real collections); `collection.<handle>.json` recorded for a bounded subset (merch collections + top-15 by `productsCount`, 20 total)
36	Recording all 250 collections' product listings would mean ~250 sequential throttled requests (~2+ minutes) for fixture purposes alone, most of which are narrow marketing/filter collections. `collections.json` is recorded as the real, complete, unmodified response (public data, nothing stripped). Only a bounded, real subset gets its `/collections/<handle>/products.json` recorded. To avoid the "missing fixture file" per-collection scenario (store-collector spec) firing ~230 times and flooding `methodology.limits`, Lane A's offline collection-membership pass should emit **one aggregated** limit line (e.g. `"collection membership recorded for 20/250 collections in fixtures; rest treated as empty (fixture-recording bound, not a live-scan limitation)"`) instead of one line per missing handle. This only applies to fixtures/offline mode — a real online scan (`collect()`) still attempts every collection subject to `maxProducts`/robots/time, so the real run Ashish does later is not artificially bounded to 20.
37	
38	### D-04. `src/types.ts` additions beyond the literal design.md §2 listing
39	Added two zod schemas design.md described only in prose: `AvailabilityDelta` (shape given in design.md §9) and `BeaconConfig` (shape given in design.md §5, referenced by name in §10's `ScanOptions.config` and function signatures but never given a zod schema). `Findings.delta` stays `z.any().optional()` exactly as design.md §2 specifies (not tightened to `AvailabilityDelta`, to stay verbatim on the frozen block). Every schema, including the two additions, has a matching `z.infer` export.
40	
41	### D-05. Report internal function names: `renderHtml` / `toCsv` / `toTerminal` (not `writeCsv`/`printTerminal` as WO §3 Lane 0 text lists)
42	WO §1's Lane 0 prompt text names the stub set `(collect, collectOffline, samplePdpMarkers, analyse, diff, writeCsv, renderHtml, printTerminal)`, but WO §3's own Lane C prompt and the report-and-cli spec both specify `renderHtml(findings): string`, `toCsv(findings): string`, `toTerminal(findings): string` as pure functions with no I/O (the "write"/"print" framing in the Lane 0 list is describing what the CLI *does with* the string, not the function name). Used the Lane C/spec names for the actual stub and library wiring, since that's the authoritative, more detailed contract and matches "pure functions returning strings" — `src/cli.ts` (Lane C) is what writes/prints.
43	
44	## 2026-09-22 — Lane A
45	
46	### D-06. `StoreSnapshot` has no field for collector-discovered limit notes — added a non-schema `collectorLimits: string[]` passthrough property instead of editing `types.ts`
47	The store-collector spec repeatedly requires the collector to *record* a limit note (robots-disallowed collection positions; product-catalogue truncation; D-03's one aggregated fixture-bound note; D-02's policies-not-checked note), and `Findings.methodology.limits` is exactly the field these are meant to end up in — but that field lives on `Findings`, which only `engine/index.ts` (`analyse()`, Lane B) constructs, and `StoreSnapshot` (design.md §2, frozen) has no `limits`/notes field of its own to carry them from the collector to the engine.
48	
49	Rather than edit the frozen `StoreSnapshot` schema, `collect()`/`collectOffline()` return an object that is a valid `StoreSnapshot` in every sense `StoreSnapshot.parse(...)` checks (zod's default `strip` mode silently drops unrecognised keys, so `.parse()` succeeds unchanged) **plus** an extra runtime-only property, `collectorLimits: string[]`, holding every note the collector itself produced. TypeScript allows this without a type error because both functions return a variable typed as `StoreSnapshot & { collectorLimits: string[] }` through a `Promise<StoreSnapshot>`-declared signature — structural widening on return, not a literal excess-property check. `tests/collector.test.ts` asserts on `snapshot.collectorLimits` directly (pre-`.parse()`) for every scenario that produces a note.
50	
51	**Proposed contract diff for Lane I / a future design.md revision:** add an optional field to `StoreSnapshot` in design.md §2 — `collectorLimits: z.array(z.string()).optional()` — so this is a first-class, typed part of the contract instead of a documented convention. Until then: **Lane B's `analyse()` should read `(snapshot as any as { collectorLimits?: string[] }).collectorLimits ?? []` and fold it into `Findings.methodology.limits` alongside whatever the engine derives on its own.** If Lane B ran before this note was visible (parallel lanes), Lane I should wire this at integration — it's a one-line addition to `engine/index.ts`.
52	
53	### D-07. Online pagination stop rule: a short page (`batch.length < limit`) also ends pagination, not only a strictly empty page
54	The store-collector spec's own "Store with 612 products" scenario expects exactly 3 product-page requests for 612 products at `limit=250` (250+250+112). That only holds if pagination stops as soon as a page returns fewer than `limit` items — a literal "until an empty page" reading would require a 4th, confirmatory, empty page fetch that the scenario's request count doesn't include. Implemented `fetchAllProducts`/`fetchAllCollections`/`fetchCollectionMembership` (`src/collector/shopify.ts`) to stop on `batch.length === 0 || batch.length < limit`. This is also the more standard real-world pagination approach (Shopify's `/products.json` never returns a short-then-nonempty sequence in practice). `collectOffline()`'s file-based loop is unaffected — it stops on a missing page file or an empty batch, which naturally matches this store's real `products.page1.json` (190, i.e. already short) followed by the explicitly-recorded empty `products.page2.json`.
55	
56	### D-08. Minor additive (backward-compatible) option surface changes in Lane A's own files
57	- `collectOffline(dir, opts?: { onProgress?, now?, config? })` — Lane 0's stub signature was `collectOffline(dir: string): Promise<StoreSnapshot>`; added an **optional** second parameter so the function is independently progress-reporting/deterministic-clock testable. `src/index.ts`'s existing call site (`collectOffline(opts.offlineFixturesDir)`, one argument) is untouched and still type-checks.
58	- `CollectOptions.now?: () => Date` — added for the same reason to `collect()`'s options; note `src/index.ts`'s `scanStore()` does not currently thread its own `opts.now` down into the `collect(url, {...})` call it makes (only into `analyseSnapshot`/`analyse`), so live scans still use wall-clock `fetchedAt` regardless — flagging in case Lane I wants `scanStore` to pass it through for full determinism in offline/replay scenarios.
59	
60	## 2026-09-22 — Lane B
61	
62	### D-06. `pdp/colour-variants-without-image` severity reuses `thresholds.lowImagePct`

# Decisions made during build (WO-BEACON-01)

Per WO §0: "Where the inputs are silent, choose the simplest option, write the choice into this file, and continue." Per Hard Rule #2: a lane needing a contract change logs the proposed diff here; the orchestrator resolves at integration. All entries below are timestamped and attributed to the lane that made the call.

## 2026-09-22 — Lane 0

### D-01. Store pick: bluetokaicoffee.com (fallback: gymshark.com)
PRD §6's literal "≥30% products with multi-option variants (size/colour)" Must criterion — read as "≥2 option axes per product" — is not met by **any** shortlisted or fallback store (verified empirically, not assumed): most Indian DTC catalogues split colour into separate product listings and carry a single option axis (or none). Raw findings:

| Host | Products | Sold-out variants | Options≥2 axes | Products w/ a real size-type option | Merch collection | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| beminimalist.co | 79 | 7.5% | 0% | — | yes | count just under 80 |
| plumgoodness.com | 414 | 3.0% | 0% | — | yes | sold-out % too low |
| mcaffeine.com | 185 | 3.8% | 0% | — | yes | sold-out % too low |
| bombayshavingcompany.com | 214 | 17.5% | 0% | 1.4% | yes | almost all single-variant SKUs |
| sleepyowl.co | 74 | 30.1% | 9.5% | 8.1% | yes | count just under 80 |
| **bluetokaicoffee.com** | **190** | **21.2%** | 28.9% | **67.9%** | **yes** | picked |
| boat-lifestyle.com | 800 (capped) | 65.2% | 1.1% | 1% | yes | colour-only variants; implausibly high sold-out % for a demo |
| thesouledstore.com | — | — | — | — | — | `/products.json` returns 200 but non-JSON — not Shopify (or storefront proxy blocks bots); disqualified |
| snitch.co.in | — | — | — | — | — | robots.txt disallows `/products.json` for `*`; disqualified |
| gymshark.com (fallback) | 800 (capped) | 55.1% | 0%* | 99.9% | yes | *colour is a separate product per style; global brand, not Indian-context (Prefer) |
| allbirds.com (fallback) | 294 | 79.5% | 0%* | 99.7% | yes | *same pattern; 79.5% sold-out looks extreme for a demo |

I used **"% of products with a genuine size-type option"** (name matches `/size|sz|waist/i` or values resolve mostly to a known/ordinal size set) as the operative richness signal instead of the literal "≥2 option axes" reading, since that's what actually drives the variant-selection (size-curve) scorecard check design.md §4 describes, and because the literal reading is unmet everywhere. This is a spike finding, not scope creep: the Must criterion itself is unsatisfiable as literally written against real Shopify catalogues in this shortlist.

**Pick: bluetokaicoffee.com.** Rationale: real, moderate (not implausible) sold-out rate (21.2%), strong size-option depth (67.9%, avg ~5 variants/product) for a meaningful variant-selection story, active merch collections (`coffee-beans`, `best-sellers-nav`, `best-selling-collection`, `bestsellers`, `new-to-coffee`), Indian DTC context (PRD §6 Prefer), and generic back-in-stock capture markers present without Swym branding — which makes the intent-capture finding land as "you have *a* capture mechanism, not Swym" rather than a null result either way. **Fallback: gymshark.com** — meets the literal Must table better on raw numbers but fails the Indian-context Prefer and both fallbacks (gymshark, allbirds) show sold-out rates (55–80%) that would look exaggerated/implausible on spot-check, hurting PRD §9's "believable when spot-checked" success criterion.

Per WO §2: posting this pick and proceeding without waiting for `go <host>`, per the WO's own contingency ("if no answer arrives within the session, proceed with the pick and flag it at the top of the final report"). Flagged at the top of the final report; easy to swap by re-running the spike against a different host if Ashish disagrees.

### D-02. Schema fix: `StoreSnapshot.policies.{shipping,refund}` made nullable
bluetokaicoffee.com's `robots.txt` disallows `/policies/*` and `/*/policies/*` for user-agent `*` (a store-specific customisation — the other 5 stores checked have no such rule). The collector must not fetch those paths (WO Hard Rule #3, store-collector spec "Robots and rate limits"). design.md §2 originally typed `policies.shipping`/`policies.refund` as plain non-nullable booleans, which cannot distinguish "confirmed missing" from "not checked because robots.txt disallows it" — collapsing them to `false` would be a factually wrong claim (I confirmed both policy pages return 200 by direct request; the collector just isn't allowed to check them). Fixed **before** any lane started building: `shipping`/`refund` are now `z.boolean().nullable()`, `null` meaning "not checked." `linkedFromHome` is unaffected (computed from the already-fetched homepage HTML, no extra disallowed fetch needed).

Consequence for Lane B (`engine/scorecard.ts`, Trust finding): treat `null` as its own case — `severity: "low"`, evidence names the robots.txt rule, recommendation notes that this also blocks any bot/agent that honours robots.txt (including AI shopping agents) from verifying the merchant's own policies. Only score `"high"` when a policy is confirmedly `false` (fetched, non-200), `"medium"` when present but not linked from home, `"none"` when both present and linked.

### D-03. Fixtures: `collections.json` kept complete (250 real collections); `collection.<handle>.json` recorded for a bounded subset (merch collections + top-15 by `productsCount`, 20 total)
Recording all 250 collections' product listings would mean ~250 sequential throttled requests (~2+ minutes) for fixture purposes alone, most of which are narrow marketing/filter collections. `collections.json` is recorded as the real, complete, unmodified response (public data, nothing stripped). Only a bounded, real subset gets its `/collections/<handle>/products.json` recorded. To avoid the "missing fixture file" per-collection scenario (store-collector spec) firing ~230 times and flooding `methodology.limits`, Lane A's offline collection-membership pass should emit **one aggregated** limit line (e.g. `"collection membership recorded for 20/250 collections in fixtures; rest treated as empty (fixture-recording bound, not a live-scan limitation)"`) instead of one line per missing handle. This only applies to fixtures/offline mode — a real online scan (`collect()`) still attempts every collection subject to `maxProducts`/robots/time, so the real run Ashish does later is not artificially bounded to 20.

### D-04. `src/types.ts` additions beyond the literal design.md §2 listing
Added two zod schemas design.md described only in prose: `AvailabilityDelta` (shape given in design.md §9) and `BeaconConfig` (shape given in design.md §5, referenced by name in §10's `ScanOptions.config` and function signatures but never given a zod schema). `Findings.delta` stays `z.any().optional()` exactly as design.md §2 specifies (not tightened to `AvailabilityDelta`, to stay verbatim on the frozen block). Every schema, including the two additions, has a matching `z.infer` export.

### D-05. Report internal function names: `renderHtml` / `toCsv` / `toTerminal` (not `writeCsv`/`printTerminal` as WO §3 Lane 0 text lists)
WO §1's Lane 0 prompt text names the stub set `(collect, collectOffline, samplePdpMarkers, analyse, diff, writeCsv, renderHtml, printTerminal)`, but WO §3's own Lane C prompt and the report-and-cli spec both specify `renderHtml(findings): string`, `toCsv(findings): string`, `toTerminal(findings): string` as pure functions with no I/O (the "write"/"print" framing in the Lane 0 list is describing what the CLI *does with* the string, not the function name). Used the Lane C/spec names for the actual stub and library wiring, since that's the authoritative, more detailed contract and matches "pure functions returning strings" — `src/cli.ts` (Lane C) is what writes/prints.

## 2026-09-22 — Lane A

### D-06. `StoreSnapshot` has no field for collector-discovered limit notes — added a non-schema `collectorLimits: string[]` passthrough property instead of editing `types.ts`
The store-collector spec repeatedly requires the collector to *record* a limit note (robots-disallowed collection positions; product-catalogue truncation; D-03's one aggregated fixture-bound note; D-02's policies-not-checked note), and `Findings.methodology.limits` is exactly the field these are meant to end up in — but that field lives on `Findings`, which only `engine/index.ts` (`analyse()`, Lane B) constructs, and `StoreSnapshot` (design.md §2, frozen) has no `limits`/notes field of its own to carry them from the collector to the engine.

Rather than edit the frozen `StoreSnapshot` schema, `collect()`/`collectOffline()` return an object that is a valid `StoreSnapshot` in every sense `StoreSnapshot.parse(...)` checks (zod's default `strip` mode silently drops unrecognised keys, so `.parse()` succeeds unchanged) **plus** an extra runtime-only property, `collectorLimits: string[]`, holding every note the collector itself produced. TypeScript allows this without a type error because both functions return a variable typed as `StoreSnapshot & { collectorLimits: string[] }` through a `Promise<StoreSnapshot>`-declared signature — structural widening on return, not a literal excess-property check. `tests/collector.test.ts` asserts on `snapshot.collectorLimits` directly (pre-`.parse()`) for every scenario that produces a note.

**Proposed contract diff for Lane I / a future design.md revision:** add an optional field to `StoreSnapshot` in design.md §2 — `collectorLimits: z.array(z.string()).optional()` — so this is a first-class, typed part of the contract instead of a documented convention. Until then: **Lane B's `analyse()` should read `(snapshot as any as { collectorLimits?: string[] }).collectorLimits ?? []` and fold it into `Findings.methodology.limits` alongside whatever the engine derives on its own.** If Lane B ran before this note was visible (parallel lanes), Lane I should wire this at integration — it's a one-line addition to `engine/index.ts`.

### D-07. Online pagination stop rule: a short page (`batch.length < limit`) also ends pagination, not only a strictly empty page
The store-collector spec's own "Store with 612 products" scenario expects exactly 3 product-page requests for 612 products at `limit=250` (250+250+112). That only holds if pagination stops as soon as a page returns fewer than `limit` items — a literal "until an empty page" reading would require a 4th, confirmatory, empty page fetch that the scenario's request count doesn't include. Implemented `fetchAllProducts`/`fetchAllCollections`/`fetchCollectionMembership` (`src/collector/shopify.ts`) to stop on `batch.length === 0 || batch.length < limit`. This is also the more standard real-world pagination approach (Shopify's `/products.json` never returns a short-then-nonempty sequence in practice). `collectOffline()`'s file-based loop is unaffected — it stops on a missing page file or an empty batch, which naturally matches this store's real `products.page1.json` (190, i.e. already short) followed by the explicitly-recorded empty `products.page2.json`.

### D-08. Minor additive (backward-compatible) option surface changes in Lane A's own files
- `collectOffline(dir, opts?: { onProgress?, now?, config? })` — Lane 0's stub signature was `collectOffline(dir: string): Promise<StoreSnapshot>`; added an **optional** second parameter so the function is independently progress-reporting/deterministic-clock testable. `src/index.ts`'s existing call site (`collectOffline(opts.offlineFixturesDir)`, one argument) is untouched and still type-checks.
- `CollectOptions.now?: () => Date` — added for the same reason to `collect()`'s options; note `src/index.ts`'s `scanStore()` does not currently thread its own `opts.now` down into the `collect(url, {...})` call it makes (only into `analyseSnapshot`/`analyse`), so live scans still use wall-clock `fetchedAt` regardless — flagging in case Lane I wants `scanStore` to pass it through for full determinism in offline/replay scenarios.

## 2026-09-22 — Lane B

### D-06. `pdp/colour-variants-without-image` severity reuses `thresholds.lowImagePct`
`design.md §4` lists exactly seven threshold config keys (`orphanPct, soldOutTopN, soldOutInTopCount, lowImagePct, shortDescPct, coreSizeOutPct, noCapturePct`) for eight required scorecard Findings — there is no dedicated key for `pdp/colour-variants-without-image`, and `beacon.config.json` (§5) confirms the same seven keys, not eight. Rather than inventing an unconfigured eighth threshold (which the frozen `BeaconConfig` zod schema in `src/types.ts` doesn't have a slot for either, and that schema is frozen per Hard Rule #2), `src/engine/scorecard.ts`'s `colourVariantsWithoutImageFinding()` reuses `config.thresholds.lowImagePct` to grade severity: both checks are in the same "PDP image completeness" family (one counts products with <2 images overall, the other counts colour-option products missing a per-variant image), so sharing one threshold pair is a reasonable reading rather than a schema change. No spec Scenario pins an exact severity value for this check, so this choice is unverified against a numeric assertion — flagged here for Lane I / Ashish in case a dedicated `colourVariantsPct` threshold is wanted in a follow-up change.

# Beacon Friction Scanner (MVP)

> **Store pick flagged, not yet approved.** The spike (`docs/spike-store-selection.md`) picked **{{STORE_HOST}}** (fallback: **{{STORE_HOST_FALLBACK}}**) against the criteria in `docs/PRD.md §6`, and — per the work order's own contingency — proceeded without waiting on a reply. Full reasoning, including a criterion reinterpretation, is in `docs/decisions-during-build.md` (D-01). Swap the host below if a different store is preferred; re-running the spike against another candidate is cheap.

Beacon scans a Shopify store's public storefront data and tells a merchant which sold-out products are leaking the most demand, in what order to restock them, and where else in the shopper journey that intent is going missing.

## Headline finding

From the first real run against `{{STORE_HOST}}` (full report: [`out/EXAMPLE/report.html`]({{EXAMPLE_REPORT_LINK}})):

- **{{HEADLINE_1}}** products are fully sold out while still sitting in a merchandised collection — the clearest form of intent leaking to a dead end.
- **{{HEADLINE_2}}** of those sold-out product pages have no back-in-stock capture at all, so the intent that reaches them is lost rather than queued.
- Top of the restock list: **{{HEADLINE_3}}** — see the top-10 table in the report for the rest, each with the components behind its score.

These are indices, not revenue figures — public storefront data has no order-volume signal, so nothing here is stated in currency (see [MVP boundary](#mvp-boundary) and Assumption A3 below).

![Example report screenshot](docs/img/report.png)

*(Screenshot of the real `report.html` run — generated by Lane I; if you're reading this before that step ran, the image above won't resolve yet.)*

## Quick start

```bash
npm i
npx beacon scan https://{{STORE_HOST}}
```

This writes a timestamped run to `out/{{STORE_HOST}}/<ISO-timestamp>/`: `snapshot.json`, `findings.json`, `restock_priority.csv`, `report.html` (open it directly, no server needed), and a terminal summary of the three headline numbers plus the top 10 restock rows. First run takes under five minutes on a normal connection; a `.cache/` directory keeps re-runs fast and under the same request budget.

**Programmatic use** — the CLI is a thin wrapper around the same library call:

```js
import { scanStore } from "beacon-scan";

const { findings } = await scanStore("https://{{STORE_HOST}}");
console.log(findings.headline);
console.log(findings.restock[0]); // top restock priority row
```

## Where the rest of the exercise lives

| Part | Location |
|---|---|
| Example report (real run) | [`out/EXAMPLE/report.html`]({{EXAMPLE_REPORT_LINK}}) |
| Part 2 — architecture (NL query at 50K-store scale) | [`docs/part2-architecture.md`](docs/part2-architecture.md) |
| Part 2 — defensibility (standalone product or Shopify feature) | [`docs/part2-defensibility.md`](docs/part2-defensibility.md) |
| Part 3 — discovery and prioritisation framework | [`docs/part3-discovery.md`](docs/part3-discovery.md) |
| AI workflow (how this was built, with Claude Code) | [`docs/ai-workflow/README.md`](docs/ai-workflow/README.md) |
| Loom walkthrough (≤3 min) | {{LOOM_LINK}} |
| PDF mirror of this write-up | {{PDF_LINK}} (see [`scripts/export-pdf.md`](scripts/export-pdf.md) to regenerate it) |

## MVP boundary

This is a deliberately bounded MVP. The following is what it does **not** do, quoted verbatim from the locked PRD (`docs/PRD.md §1`) — this is the honest list of reasons Swym couldn't use this as-is:

- **N1.** No hosted service, scheduler, multi-store, auth, database server, or UI beyond a static HTML report.
- **N2.** No runtime LLM. The NL-query layer is designed in `docs/part2-architecture.md`, not implemented.
- **N3.** No Swym data integration; no assumptions about Swym internals.
- **N4.** Scoring is a transparent v0 heuristic with weights in one config file; no calibration, no ML.
- **N5.** Only two friction families are scored in depth (Demand Leakage, Variant/PDP hygiene); the other journey stages get 1–2 cheap presence checks each.
- **N6.** No PDP screenshotting, no headless browser, no review-platform scraping.
- **N7.** No API keys, auth, tenancy, or hosted API. The code is **library-first** (`import { scanStore } from "beacon-scan"`) with the CLI as a thin wrapper, so the shape of an eventual SDK is visible; keys/tenancy/rate plans are designed in `docs/part2-architecture.md`, not built. Public-data scanning has nothing to authenticate, and a working key system would make this adoptable as-is.

## Assumptions

From `docs/PRD.md §7`, stated here because a reviewer running this against a different store should know what's being taken on faith:

- **A1.** Public storefront JSON reflects live availability (Shopify serves it from the same catalogue; it can lag by minutes).
- **A2.** Collection order approximates merchandising intent; "bestseller"-style handles approximate demand.
- **A3.** A sold-out variant on a merchandised product is intent lost; the scan cannot see how much.
- **A4.** Detection of back-in-stock capture by HTML markers is approximate — themes vary.
- **A5.** The reviewer runs on macOS/Linux with Node ≥20.

## What the scan checks

One headline score (Restock Priority / Demand Leakage) plus a five-stage journey scorecard, all from public data only — `/products.json`, `/collections.json`, per-collection product listings, and a throttled sample of sold-out product pages. `docs/PRD.md §3` has the full scoring formula and weights; `beacon.config.json` holds the weights themselves, in one file, so the heuristic isn't buried in code.

| Stage | What's checked |
|---|---|
| Discovery | Orphan products (in no collection); sold-out products sitting in top collection positions |
| PDP | Products with fewer than 2 images; short descriptions; colour variants missing an image |
| Variant selection | Size-curve holes — whether the *middle* sizes, not just the edges, are sold out |
| Intent capture | Sampled sold-out PDPs checked for a back-in-stock signup mechanism |
| Trust | Shipping/refund policy pages present and linked from the homepage — or, if `robots.txt` disallows checking them, that's stated rather than guessed |

Every finding in the report carries its evidence (endpoint and field) and a recommendation — nothing is asserted without a source.

# Beacon Friction Scanner (MVP)

> **Store pick flagged, not yet approved.** The spike (`docs/spike-store-selection.md`) picked **{{STORE_HOST}}** (fallback: **{{STORE_HOST_FALLBACK}}**) against the criteria in `docs/PRD.md §6`, and — per the work order's own contingency — proceeded without waiting on a reply. Full reasoning, including a criterion reinterpretation, is in `docs/decisions-during-build.md` (D-01). Swap the host below if a different store is preferred; re-running the spike against another candidate is cheap.

Beacon scans a Shopify store's public storefront data and tells a merchant which sold-out products are leaking the most demand, in what order to restock them, and where else in the shopper journey that intent is going missing.

## Headline finding

From the first real run against `{{STORE_HOST}}` (full report: [`out/EXAMPLE/report.html`]({{EXAMPLE_REPORT_LINK}})):

- **{{HEADLINE_1}}** products are fully sold out while still sitting in a merchandised collection — the clearest form of intent leaking to a dead end.
- **{{HEADLINE_2}}** of those sold-out product pages have no back-in-stock capture at all, so the intent that reaches them is lost rather than queued.
- Top of the restock list: **{{HEADLINE_3}}** — see the top-10 table in the report for the rest, each with the components behind its score.

These are indices, not revenue figures — public storefront data has no order-volume signal, so nothing here is stated in currency (see [MVP boundary](#mvp-boundary) and Assumption A3 below).

![Example report screenshot](docs/img/report.png)

*(Screenshot of the real `report.html` run — generated by Lane I; if you're reading this before that step ran, the image above won't resolve yet.)*

## Quick start

```bash
npm i
npx beacon scan https://{{STORE_HOST}}
```

This writes a timestamped run to `out/{{STORE_HOST}}/<ISO-timestamp>/`: `snapshot.json`, `findings.json`, `restock_priority.csv`, `report.html` (open it directly, no server needed), and a terminal summary of the three headline numbers plus the top 10 restock rows. First run takes under five minutes on a normal connection; a `.cache/` directory keeps re-runs fast and under the same request budget.

**Programmatic use** — the CLI is a thin wrapper around the same library call:

```js
import { scanStore } from "beacon-scan";

const { findings } = await scanStore("https://{{STORE_HOST}}");
console.log(findings.headline);
console.log(findings.restock[0]); // top restock priority row
```

## Where the rest of the exercise lives

| Example report (real run) | [`out/EXAMPLE/report.html`]({{EXAMPLE_REPORT_LINK}}) |

## MVP boundary

This is a deliberately bounded MVP. The following is what it does **not** do, quoted verbatim from the locked PRD (`docs/PRD.md §1`) — this is the honest list of reasons Swym couldn't use this as-is:

- **N1.** No hosted service, scheduler, multi-store, auth, database server, or UI beyond a static HTML report.
- **N2.** No runtime LLM. The NL-query layer is designed in `docs/part2-architecture.md`, not implemented.
- **N3.** No Swym data integration; no assumptions about Swym internals.
- **N4.** Scoring is a transparent v0 heuristic with weights in one config file; no calibration, no ML.
- **N5.** Only two friction families are scored in depth (Demand Leakage, Variant/PDP hygiene); the other journey stages get 1–2 cheap presence checks each.
- **N6.** No PDP screenshotting, no headless browser, no review-platform scraping.
- **N7.** No API keys, auth, tenancy, or hosted API. The code is **library-first** (`import { scanStore } from "beacon-scan"`) with the CLI as a thin wrapper, so the shape of an eventual SDK is visible; keys/tenancy/rate plans are designed in `docs/part2-architecture.md`, not built. Public-data scanning has nothing to authenticate, and a working key system would make this adoptable as-is.

## Assumptions

From `docs/PRD.md §7`, stated here because a reviewer running this against a different store should know what's being taken on faith:

- **A1.** Public storefront JSON reflects live availability (Shopify serves it from the same catalogue; it can lag by minutes).
- **A2.** Collection order approximates merchandising intent; "bestseller"-style handles approximate demand.
- **A3.** A sold-out variant on a merchandised product is intent lost; the scan cannot see how much.
- **A4.** Detection of back-in-stock capture by HTML markers is approximate — themes vary.
- **A5.** The reviewer runs on macOS/Linux with Node ≥20.

## What the scan checks

One headline score (Restock Priority / Demand Leakage) plus a five-stage journey scorecard, all from public data only — `/products.json`, `/collections.json`, per-collection product listings, and a throttled sample of sold-out product pages. `docs/PRD.md §3` has the full scoring formula and weights; `beacon.config.json` holds the weights themselves, in one file, so the heuristic isn't buried in code.

| Stage | What's checked |
|---|---|
| Discovery | Orphan products (in no collection); sold-out products sitting in top collection positions |
| PDP | Products with fewer than 2 images; short descriptions; colour variants missing an image |
| Variant selection | Size-curve holes — whether the *middle* sizes, not just the edges, are sold out |
| Intent capture | Sampled sold-out PDPs checked for a back-in-stock signup mechanism |
| Trust | Shipping/refund policy pages present and linked from the homepage — or, if `robots.txt` disallows checking them, that's stated rather than guessed |

Every finding in the report carries its evidence (endpoint and field) and a recommendation — nothing is asserted without a source.

| Part | Location |
|---|---|
| Example report (real run) | [`out/EXAMPLE/report.html`]({{EXAMPLE_REPORT_LINK}}) |
| Part 2 — architecture (NL query at 50K-store scale) | [`docs/part2-architecture.md`](docs/part2-architecture.md) |

| AI workflow (how this was built, with Claude Code) | [`docs/ai-workflow/README.md`](docs/ai-workflow/README.md) |
| Loom walkthrough (≤3 min) | {{LOOM_LINK}} |
| PDF mirror of this write-up | {{PDF_LINK}} (see [`scripts/export-pdf.md`](scripts/export-pdf.md) to regenerate it) |

## MVP boundary

This is a deliberately bounded MVP. The following is what it does **not** do, quoted verbatim from the locked PRD (`docs/PRD.md §1`) — this is the honest list of reasons Swym couldn't use this as-is:

- **N1.** No hosted service, scheduler, multi-store, auth, database server, or UI beyond a static HTML report.
- **N2.** No runtime LLM. The NL-query layer is designed in `docs/part2-architecture.md`, not implemented.
- **N3.** No Swym data integration; no assumptions about Swym internals.
- **N4.** Scoring is a transparent v0 heuristic with weights in one config file; no calibration, no ML.
- **N5.** Only two friction families are scored in depth (Demand Leakage, Variant/PDP hygiene); the other journey stages get 1–2 cheap presence checks each.
- **N6.** No PDP screenshotting, no headless browser, no review-platform scraping.
- **N7.** No API keys, auth, tenancy, or hosted API. The code is **library-first** (`import { scanStore } from "beacon-scan"`) with the CLI as a thin wrapper, so the shape of an eventual SDK is visible; keys/tenancy/rate plans are designed in `docs/part2-architecture.md`, not built. Public-data scanning has nothing to authenticate, and a working key system would make this adoptable as-is.

## Assumptions

From `docs/PRD.md §7`, stated here because a reviewer running this against a different store should know what's being taken on faith:

- **A1.** Public storefront JSON reflects live availability (Shopify serves it from the same catalogue; it can lag by minutes).
- **A2.** Collection order approximates merchandising intent; "bestseller"-style handles approximate demand.
- **A3.** A sold-out variant on a merchandised product is intent lost; the scan cannot see how much.
- **A4.** Detection of back-in-stock capture by HTML markers is approximate — themes vary.
- **A5.** The reviewer runs on macOS/Linux with Node ≥20.

## What the scan checks

One headline score (Restock Priority / Demand Leakage) plus a five-stage journey scorecard, all from public data only — `/products.json`, `/collections.json`, per-collection product listings, and a throttled sample of sold-out product pages. `docs/PRD.md §3` has the full scoring formula and weights; `beacon.config.json` holds the weights themselves, in one file, so the heuristic isn't buried in code.

| Stage | What's checked |
|---|---|
| Discovery | Orphan products (in no collection); sold-out products sitting in top collection positions |
| PDP | Products with fewer than 2 images; short descriptions; colour variants missing an image |
| Variant selection | Size-curve holes — whether the *middle* sizes, not just the edges, are sold out |
| Intent capture | Sampled sold-out PDPs checked for a back-in-stock signup mechanism |
| Trust | Shipping/refund policy pages present and linked from the homepage — or, if `robots.txt` disallows checking them, that's stated rather than guessed |

Every finding in the report carries its evidence (endpoint and field) and a recommendation — nothing is asserted without a source.

## 2026-09-22 — Lane I (post-integration, first real run)

### D-10. `http.ts`: added a shared cooldown gate so a 429 pauses the whole client, not just the retrying request
First real (online) scan failed hard: `RATE_LIMITED` on collection #207/225 (`test-coffee-maker`) after 206 successful sequential collection-membership fetches. Root cause found in `src/collector/http.ts`: the token bucket throttles how fast *new* requests are issued, but with `concurrency: 2`, while one request was mid-backoff from a 429, its sibling slot kept pulling fresh URLs from the queue and firing them at the normal rate — so the client never actually slowed down as a whole once the store started rate-limiting, and the per-request exponential backoff (1s→16s, max 4 retries, matching `openspec/project.md`'s "Important Constraints" exactly) couldn't outrun a sustained 429 state being kept alive by the other slot.

Fix: added a shared `cooldownUntil` timestamp inside `createHttp()`'s closure. Every 429/5xx retry sets `cooldownUntil = max(cooldownUntil, now() + waitMs)` (honouring `Retry-After` when the store sends one, same as before), and `executeThrottled()` now waits out any active cooldown *before* taking a token bucket slot — for every request, not just the one that got the 429. This changes no configured value (`rps`/`concurrency`/`maxRetries`/`timeoutMs` in `beacon.config.json`, frozen per Hard Rule #2 / design.md §5, are untouched) — it's a behavioural fix to how concurrency and backoff interact, keeping the existing numbers but making them behave as "polite" as the spec intends. `tests/collector.test.ts` (36/36) unaffected.

Recovery: the failed run's 6h disk cache (`.cache/bluetokaicoffee.com/`, 207 files) already held every successful response, so the retry after this fix reuses those and only needs the ~19 remaining collections — no need to re-fetch from scratch or to bound the online path's collection count (which would contradict D-03's explicit statement that the real run is *not* artificially bounded to a small collection subset the way offline fixtures are).
DECLOG

6	
7	### D-01. Store pick: bluetokaicoffee.com (fallback: gymshark.com)
8	PRD §6's literal "≥30% products with multi-option variants (size/colour)" Must criterion — read as "≥2 option axes per product" — is not met by **any** shortlisted or fallback store (verified empirically, not assumed): most Indian DTC catalogues split colour into separate product listings and carry a single option axis (or none). Raw findings:
9	
10	| Host | Products | Sold-out variants | Options≥2 axes | Products w/ a real size-type option | Merch collection | Notes |
11	|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
12	| beminimalist.co | 79 | 7.5% | 0% | — | yes | count just under 80 |
13	| plumgoodness.com | 414 | 3.0% | 0% | — | yes | sold-out % too low |
14	| mcaffeine.com | 185 | 3.8% | 0% | — | yes | sold-out % too low |
15	| bombayshavingcompany.com | 214 | 17.5% | 0% | 1.4% | yes | almost all single-variant SKUs |
16	| sleepyowl.co | 74 | 30.1% | 9.5% | 8.1% | yes | count just under 80 |
17	| **bluetokaicoffee.com** | **190** | **21.2%** | 28.9% | **67.9%** | **yes** | picked |
18	| boat-lifestyle.com | 800 (capped) | 65.2% | 1.1% | 1% | yes | colour-only variants; implausibly high sold-out % for a demo |
19	| thesouledstore.com | — | — | — | — | — | `/products.json` returns 200 but non-JSON — not Shopify (or storefront proxy blocks bots); disqualified |
20	| snitch.co.in | — | — | — | — | — | robots.txt disallows `/products.json` for `*`; disqualified |
21	| gymshark.com (fallback) | 800 (capped) | 55.1% | 0%* | 99.9% | yes | *colour is a separate product per style; global brand, not Indian-context (Prefer) |
22	| allbirds.com (fallback) | 294 | 79.5% | 0%* | 99.7% | yes | *same pattern; 79.5% sold-out looks extreme for a demo |
23	
24	I used **"% of products with a genuine size-type option"** (name matches `/size|sz|waist/i` or values resolve mostly to a known/ordinal size set) as the operative richness signal instead of the literal "≥2 option axes" reading, since that's what actually drives the variant-selection (size-curve) scorecard check design.md §4 describes, and because the literal reading is unmet everywhere. This is a spike finding, not scope creep: the Must criterion itself is unsatisfiable as literally written against real Shopify catalogues in this shortlist.
25	
26	**Pick: bluetokaicoffee.com.** Rationale: real, moderate (not implausible) sold-out rate (21.2%), strong size-option depth (67.9%, avg ~5 variants/product) for a meaningful variant-selection story, active merch collections (`coffee-beans`, `best-sellers-nav`, `best-selling-collection`, `bestsellers`, `new-to-coffee`), Indian DTC context (PRD §6 Prefer), and generic back-in-stock capture markers present without Swym branding — which makes the intent-capture finding land as "you have *a* capture mechanism, not Swym" rather than a null result either way. **Fallback: gymshark.com** — meets the literal Must table better on raw numbers but fails the Indian-context Prefer and both fallbacks (gymshark, allbirds) show sold-out rates (55–80%) that would look exaggerated/implausible on spot-check, hurting PRD §9's "believable when spot-checked" success criterion.
27	
28	Per WO §2: posting this pick and proceeding without waiting for `go <host>`, per the WO's own contingency ("if no answer arrives within the session, proceed with the pick and flag it at the top of the final report"). Flagged at the top of the final report; easy to swap by re-running the spike against a different host if Ashish disagrees.
29	
30	### D-02. Schema fix: `StoreSnapshot.policies.{shipping,refund}` made nullable
31	bluetokaicoffee.com's `robots.txt` disallows `/policies/*` and `/*/policies/*` for user-agent `*` (a store-specific customisation — the other 5 stores checked have no such rule). The collector must not fetch those paths (WO Hard Rule #3, store-collector spec "Robots and rate limits"). design.md §2 originally typed `policies.shipping`/`policies.refund` as plain non-nullable booleans, which cannot distinguish "confirmed missing" from "not checked because robots.txt disallows it" — collapsing them to `false` would be a factually wrong claim (I confirmed both policy pages return 200 by direct request; the collector just isn't allowed to check them). Fixed **before** any lane started building: `shipping`/`refund` are now `z.boolean().nullable()`, `null` meaning "not checked." `linkedFromHome` is unaffected (computed from the already-fetched homepage HTML, no extra disallowed fetch needed).
32	
33	Consequence for Lane B (`engine/scorecard.ts`, Trust finding): treat `null` as its own case — `severity: "low"`, evidence names the robots.txt rule, recommendation notes that this also blocks any bot/agent that honours robots.txt (including AI shopping agents) from verifying the merchant's own policies. Only score `"high"` when a policy is confirmedly `false` (fetched, non-200), `"medium"` when present but not linked from home, `"none"` when both present and linked.
34	
35	### D-03. Fixtures: `collections.json` kept complete (250 real collections); `collection.<handle>.json` recorded for a bounded subset (merch collections + top-15 by `productsCount`, 20 total)
36	Recording all 250 collections' product listings would mean ~250 sequential throttled requests (~2+ minutes) for fixture purposes alone, most of which are narrow marketing/filter collections. `collections.json` is recorded as the real, complete, unmodified response (public data, nothing stripped). Only a bounded, real subset gets its `/collections/<handle>/products.json` recorded. To avoid the "missing fixture file" per-collection scenario (store-collector spec) firing ~230 times and flooding `methodology.limits`, Lane A's offline collection-membership pass should emit **one aggregated** limit line (e.g. `"collection membership recorded for 20/250 collections in fixtures; rest treated as empty (fixture-recording bound, not a live-scan limitation)"`) instead of one line per missing handle. This only applies to fixtures/offline mode — a real online scan (`collect()`) still attempts every collection subject to `maxProducts`/robots/time, so the real run Ashish does later is not artificially bounded to 20.
37	
38	### D-04. `src/types.ts` additions beyond the literal design.md §2 listing
39	Added two zod schemas design.md described only in prose: `AvailabilityDelta` (shape given in design.md §9) and `BeaconConfig` (shape given in design.md §5, referenced by name in §10's `ScanOptions.config` and function signatures but never given a zod schema). `Findings.delta` stays `z.any().optional()` exactly as design.md §2 specifies (not tightened to `AvailabilityDelta`, to stay verbatim on the frozen block). Every schema, including the two additions, has a matching `z.infer` export.
40	
41	### D-05. Report internal function names: `renderHtml` / `toCsv` / `toTerminal` (not `writeCsv`/`printTerminal` as WO §3 Lane 0 text lists)
42	WO §1's Lane 0 prompt text names the stub set `(collect, collectOffline, samplePdpMarkers, analyse, diff, writeCsv, renderHtml, printTerminal)`, but WO §3's own Lane C prompt and the report-and-cli spec both specify `renderHtml(findings): string`, `toCsv(findings): string`, `toTerminal(findings): string` as pure functions with no I/O (the "write"/"print" framing in the Lane 0 list is describing what the CLI *does with* the string, not the function name). Used the Lane C/spec names for the actual stub and library wiring, since that's the authoritative, more detailed contract and matches "pure functions returning strings" — `src/cli.ts` (Lane C) is what writes/prints.

cat >> docs/decisions-during-build.md << 'DECLOG'

### D-11. `pdp-markers.ts`: a robots.txt-disallowed PDP now skips instead of aborting the whole sample
Second real-run failure, found immediately after D-10's fix let the scan get past all 225 collections: `ROBOTS_DISALLOWED` on `/products/all-products` crashed the run during PDP sampling (candidate 13/20). This store's `robots.txt` has a specific `Disallow: /products/all-products` rule (a real, deliberate store-specific rule — not a bug in our robots parser; confirmed by reading the raw cached `robots.txt`). The bug was in `samplePdpMarkers`'s online branch (`src/collector/pdp-markers.ts`): it called `http.get(product.url)` directly, and `http.get()` throws `BeaconError("ROBOTS_DISALLOWED", ...)` by design when a path is disallowed (correct — fetching a disallowed path at all would be the actual violation) — but nothing caught it, so one disallowed PDP among 20 candidates took down the entire scan. `fetchCollectionMembership` in `src/collector/shopify.ts` already had the right pattern (`http.allowed()` checked first, skip-and-continue on `false`) — `pdp-markers.ts`'s online path just didn't follow it. Fixed to match: check `allowed()` first, skip that one candidate via `onProgress` + `continue` on disallow, same as the offline path already does for a missing fixture file. No test regressions (`collector.test.ts` 36/36 still green — none of Lane A's own mocked scenarios happened to exercise a disallowed PDP mid-sample, which is why this didn't surface until the real store hit it).
DECLOG

1	# Beacon Friction Scanner (MVP)
2	
3	> **Store pick flagged, not yet approved by Ashish.** The spike (`docs/spike-store-selection.md`) picked **bluetokaicoffee.com** (fallback: **gymshark.com**) against the criteria in `docs/PRD.md §6`, and — per the work order's own contingency — proceeded without waiting on a reply. Full reasoning, including a criterion reinterpretation, is in `docs/decisions-during-build.md` (D-01). The whole pipeline (collector → engine → report → CLI) has since run end-to-end against this store's real, recorded fixtures — see the headline numbers below — but that's an **offline** run against fixtures recorded 2026-09-22, not yet the live scan from Ashish's Mac (`docs/PRD.md §10` Day 1 PM / task I.3). Swap the host below if a different store is preferred; re-running the spike against another candidate is cheap.
4	
5	Beacon scans a Shopify store's public storefront data and tells a merchant which sold-out products are leaking the most demand, in what order to restock them, and where else in the shopper journey that intent is going missing.
6

## Where the rest of the exercise lives

| Part | Location |
|---|---|
| Example report (offline fixture run — see note above) | [`out/EXAMPLE/report.html`](out/EXAMPLE/report.html) |
| Part 2 — architecture (NL query at 50K-store scale) | [`docs/part2-architecture.md`](docs/part2-architecture.md) |
| Part 2 — defensibility (standalone product or Shopify feature) | [`docs/part2-defensibility.md`](docs/part2-defensibility.md) |

| PDF mirror of this write-up | *not yet generated — see [`scripts/export-pdf.md`](scripts/export-pdf.md)* |

## MVP boundary

This is a deliberately bounded MVP. The following is what it does **not** do, quoted verbatim from the locked PRD (`docs/PRD.md §1`) — this is the honest list of reasons Swym couldn't use this as-is:

- **N1.** No hosted service, scheduler, multi-store, auth, database server, or UI beyond a static HTML report.
- **N2.** No runtime LLM. The NL-query layer is designed in `docs/part2-architecture.md`, not implemented.
- **N3.** No Swym data integration; no assumptions about Swym internals.
- **N4.** Scoring is a transparent v0 heuristic with weights in one config file; no calibration, no ML.
- **N5.** Only two friction families are scored in depth (Demand Leakage, Variant/PDP hygiene); the other journey stages get 1–2 cheap presence checks each.
- **N6.** No PDP screenshotting, no headless browser, no review-platform scraping.
- **N7.** No API keys, auth, tenancy, or hosted API. The code is **library-first** (`import { scanStore } from "beacon-scan"`) with the CLI as a thin wrapper, so the shape of an eventual SDK is visible; keys/tenancy/rate plans are designed in `docs/part2-architecture.md`, not built. Public-data scanning has nothing to authenticate, and a working key system would make this adoptable as-is.

## Assumptions

From `docs/PRD.md §7`, stated here because a reviewer running this against a different store should know what's being taken on faith:

- **A1.** Public storefront JSON reflects live availability (Shopify serves it from the same catalogue; it can lag by minutes).
- **A2.** Collection order approximates merchandising intent; "bestseller"-style handles approximate demand.
- **A3.** A sold-out variant on a merchandised product is intent lost; the scan cannot see how much.
- **A4.** Detection of back-in-stock capture by HTML markers is approximate — themes vary.
- **A5.** The reviewer runs on macOS/Linux with Node ≥20.

## What the scan checks

One headline score (Restock Priority / Demand Leakage) plus a five-stage journey scorecard, all from public data only — `/products.json`, `/collections.json`, per-collection product listings, and a throttled sample of sold-out product pages. `docs/PRD.md §3` has the full scoring formula and weights; `beacon.config.json` holds the weights themselves, in one file, so the heuristic isn't buried in code.

| Stage | What's checked |
|---|---|
| Discovery | Orphan products (in no collection); sold-out products sitting in top collection positions |
| PDP | Products with fewer than 2 images; short descriptions; colour variants missing an image |
| Variant selection | Size-curve holes — whether the *middle* sizes, not just the edges, are sold out |
| Intent capture | Sampled sold-out PDPs checked for a back-in-stock signup mechanism |
| Trust | Shipping/refund policy pages present and linked from the homepage — or, if `robots.txt` disallows checking them, that's stated rather than guessed |

Every finding in the report carries its evidence (endpoint and field) and a recommendation — nothing is asserted without a source.

| PDF mirror of this write-up | *not yet generated — see [`scripts/export-pdf.md`](scripts/export-pdf.md)* |

## MVP boundary

This is a deliberately bounded MVP. The following is what it does **not** do, quoted verbatim from the locked PRD (`docs/PRD.md §1`) — this is the honest list of reasons Swym couldn't use this as-is:

- **N1.** No hosted service, scheduler, multi-store, auth, database server, or UI beyond a static HTML report.
- **N2.** No runtime LLM. The NL-query layer is designed in `docs/part2-architecture.md`, not implemented.
- **N3.** No Swym data integration; no assumptions about Swym internals.
- **N4.** Scoring is a transparent v0 heuristic with weights in one config file; no calibration, no ML.
- **N5.** Only two friction families are scored in depth (Demand Leakage, Variant/PDP hygiene); the other journey stages get 1–2 cheap presence checks each.
- **N6.** No PDP screenshotting, no headless browser, no review-platform scraping.
- **N7.** No API keys, auth, tenancy, or hosted API. The code is **library-first** (`import { scanStore } from "beacon-scan"`) with the CLI as a thin wrapper, so the shape of an eventual SDK is visible; keys/tenancy/rate plans are designed in `docs/part2-architecture.md`, not built. Public-data scanning has nothing to authenticate, and a working key system would make this adoptable as-is.

## Assumptions

From `docs/PRD.md §7`, stated here because a reviewer running this against a different store should know what's being taken on faith:

- **A1.** Public storefront JSON reflects live availability (Shopify serves it from the same catalogue; it can lag by minutes).
- **A2.** Collection order approximates merchandising intent; "bestseller"-style handles approximate demand.
- **A3.** A sold-out variant on a merchandised product is intent lost; the scan cannot see how much.
- **A4.** Detection of back-in-stock capture by HTML markers is approximate — themes vary.
- **A5.** The reviewer runs on macOS/Linux with Node ≥20.

## What the scan checks

One headline score (Restock Priority / Demand Leakage) plus a five-stage journey scorecard, all from public data only — `/products.json`, `/collections.json`, per-collection product listings, and a throttled sample of sold-out product pages. `docs/PRD.md §3` has the full scoring formula and weights; `beacon.config.json` holds the weights themselves, in one file, so the heuristic isn't buried in code.

| Stage | What's checked |
|---|---|
| Discovery | Orphan products (in no collection); sold-out products sitting in top collection positions |
| PDP | Products with fewer than 2 images; short descriptions; colour variants missing an image |
| Variant selection | Size-curve holes — whether the *middle* sizes, not just the edges, are sold out |
| Intent capture | Sampled sold-out PDPs checked for a back-in-stock signup mechanism |
| Trust | Shipping/refund policy pages present and linked from the homepage — or, if `robots.txt` disallows checking them, that's stated rather than guessed |

Every finding in the report carries its evidence (endpoint and field) and a recommendation — nothing is asserted without a source.

## Real scan complete

Both requests done: `git init` scoped correctly to `beacon-takehome/`, and the **live** scan against `bluetokaicoffee.com` ran successfully end-to-end.

Getting there took two real bugs the offline fixtures never exercised — both found and fixed:
- **A throttling bug**: the collector's token bucket only slowed the request that got a 429, not its concurrent sibling — so once the store started rate-limiting (at collection 207/225), the client kept hammering it instead of backing off as a whole, and the run died with `RATE_LIMITED`. Fixed with a shared cooldown gate (`docs/decisions-during-build.md` D-10).
- **A hard-crash bug**: this store's robots.txt specifically disallows one product page (`/products/all-products`), and the PDP sampler let that single disallowed page abort the entire 20-page sample instead of skipping it, the way the collection-fetch code already did elsewhere. Fixed to skip-and-continue (D-11).

**Real headline numbers** (not offline fixtures anymore):
- 199/959 variants sold out across 190 products; 20 leaking demand on a merchandised collection
- 0/19 sampled sold-out PDPs lack back-in-stock capture (store has a generic mechanism, not Swym)
- Top restock pick: **Amruthavarshini Estate** (idx 0.760, 39/39 sold out) — I independently verified this is genuinely sold out on the live store right now
- Only 3/225 real collections were robots-disallowed (vs. the offline fixture's artificial 213/225 gap)

# Schedule Cloud Agents

You are helping the user schedule, update, list, or run **cloud** Claude Code agents. These are NOT local cron jobs — each routine spawns a fully isolated cloud session (CCR) in Anthropic's cloud infrastructure, either on a recurring cron schedule or once at a specific time. The agent runs in a sandboxed environment with its own git checkout, tools, and optional MCP connections.

## First Step

Your FIRST action must be a single AskUserQuestion tool call (no preamble). Use this EXACT string for the `question` field — do not paraphrase or shorten it:

"⚠ Heads-up:\n- Not in a git repo — you'll need to specify a repo URL manually (or skip repos entirely).\n- No MCP connectors for cloud routines — 1 MCP server configured in Claude Code can't be attached to routines (run /mcp to see it); routines can only use claude.ai connectors. claude.ai connectors could not be loaded in this session (the login token does not include the MCP-connectors permission); any connected on claude.ai remain available to routines there.\n\nWhat would you like to do with scheduled cloud agents?"

Set `header: "Action"` and offer the four actions (create/list/update/run) as options. After the user picks, follow the matching workflow below.


## What You Can Do

Use the `RemoteTrigger` tool (load it first with `ToolSearch select:RemoteTrigger`; auth is handled in-process — do not use curl):

- `{action: "list"}` — list all routines
- `{action: "get", trigger_id: "..."}` — fetch one routine
- `{action: "create", body: {...}}` — create a routine
- `{action: "update", trigger_id: "...", body: {...}}` — partial update
- `{action: "run", trigger_id: "..."}` — run a routine now
- `{action: "list_runs", trigger_id: "..."}` — the routine's recent run sessions, most recently active first
- `{action: "get_run_log", session_id: "..."}` — condensed log of one run (provisioning, tool calls and errors, permission denials, API retries, final result)

To debug a routine that misbehaved, call `list_runs` and then `get_run_log` on the run in question. A fire that was skipped or refused before a session existed (routine paused, a fire cap, a kill switch) or that failed its pre-creation checks (repository access, environment) leaves no run in `list_runs`, and a routine that posts into an existing session adds to that session rather than a new run; when the list is empty or short, check the routine itself with `get` rather than concluding it never fired.

(Note: the API uses `trigger_id` as the parameter name, but the user-facing term is "routine".)

You CANNOT delete routines. If the user asks to delete, direct them to: https://claude.ai/code/routines

## Create body shape

For a recurring schedule:

```json
{
  "name": "AGENT_NAME",
  "cron_expression": "CRON_EXPR",
  "enabled": true,
  "job_config": {
    "ccr": {
      "environment_id": "ENVIRONMENT_ID",
      "session_context": {
        "model": "claude-sonnet-5",
        "sources": [
          {"git_repository": {"url": "https://github.com/ORG/REPO"}}
        ],
        "allowed_tools": ["Bash", "Read", "Write", "Edit", "Glob", "Grep"]
      },
      "events": [
        {"data": {
          "uuid": "<lowercase v4 uuid>",
          "session_id": "",
          "type": "user",
          "parent_tool_use_id": null,
          "message": {"content": "PROMPT_HERE", "role": "user"}
        }}
      ]
    }
  }
}
```

For a one-time run, replace `"cron_expression": "CRON_EXPR"` with `"run_once_at": "YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SSZ"` (RFC3339 UTC, must be in the future). Everything else is identical.

Generate a fresh lowercase UUID for `events[].data.uuid` yourself.

Every `events[].data.message` must be the API message shape `{"role": "user", "content": "..."}` — the `role` field is required, never omit it. If you instead write the body in the `session_request` form that list and get return, the same rule applies to `session_request.events[].payload.message`.

## Available MCP Connectors

These are the user's currently connected claude.ai MCP connectors:

claude.ai connectors could not be loaded in this Claude Code session (the session's login token does not include the MCP-connectors permission), so none are listed here. Connectors the user has connected on claude.ai remain available to cloud routines there.
1 MCP server is configured directly in Claude Code and NOT available to routines (the user can run /mcp to see it). Routines can only use claude.ai connectors. As explained above, the claude.ai connector list was not loaded in this session, so this service may already have a connector on claude.ai that routines can use — do not assert that the user must connect one.

When attaching connectors to a routine, use the `connector_uuid` and `name` shown above (the name is already sanitized to only contain letters, numbers, hyphens, and underscores), and the connector's URL. The `name` field in `mcp_connections` must only contain `[a-zA-Z0-9_-]` — dots and spaces are NOT allowed.

**Important:** Infer what services the agent needs from the user's description. For example, if they say "check Datadog and Slack me errors," the agent needs both Datadog and Slack connectors. Cross-reference against the list above and warn if any required service isn't connected. If a needed connector is missing, direct the user to https://claude.ai/customize/connectors to connect it first.

## Environments

Every routine requires an `environment_id` in the job config. This determines where the cloud agent runs. Ask the user which environment to use.

Available environments:
- Default (id: env_014qTxLdEHQ3MbQrHWTjN2yi, kind: anthropic_cloud)

Use the `id` value as the `environment_id` in `job_config.ccr.environment_id`.


## API Field Reference

### Create Routine — Required Fields
- `name` (string) — A descriptive name
- Exactly ONE of:
  - `cron_expression` (string) — 5-field cron in UTC. **Minimum interval is 1 hour.**
  - `run_once_at` (string) — RFC3339 UTC timestamp. Must be in the future. Fires once, then auto-disables.
- `job_config` (object) — Session configuration (see structure above)

### Create Routine — Optional Fields
- `enabled` (boolean, default: true)
- `mcp_connections` (array) — MCP servers to attach:
  ```json
  [{"connector_uuid": "uuid", "name": "server-name", "url": "https://..."}]
  ```

### Update Routine — Optional Fields
All fields optional (partial update):
- `name`, `cron_expression`, `run_once_at`, `enabled`, `job_config`
- `mcp_connections` — Replace MCP connections
- `clear_mcp_connections` (boolean) — Remove all MCP connections

### Cron Expression Examples

The user's local timezone is **Asia/Calcutta**. Cron expressions and `run_once_at` timestamps are always in UTC. When the user says a local time, convert it to UTC but confirm with them: "9am Asia/Calcutta = Xam UTC, so the cron would be `0 X * * 1-5`." For one-time runs, the same conversion applies — "run this at 3pm" → `"run_once_at": "YYYY-MM-DDTHH:00:00Z"` with their 3pm converted to UTC.

- `0 9 * * 1-5` — Every weekday at 9am **UTC**
- `0 */2 * * *` — Every 2 hours
- `0 0 * * *` — Daily at midnight **UTC**
- `30 14 * * 1` — Every Monday at 2:30pm **UTC**
- `0 8 1 * *` — First of every month at 8am **UTC**

Minimum interval is 1 hour. `*/30 * * * *` will be rejected.

### Current Time (for one-off runs)

When /schedule was invoked it was **Tue, Sep 22, 2026 at 06:45 PM** (Asia/Calcutta) / **2026-09-22T13:15:55.430Z** UTC. Treat this as an approximate anchor only — the conversation may have been running for a while since then.

**Before computing any `run_once_at` value, you MUST re-check the current time** by running `date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ` via the Bash tool. Do not guess or infer today's date from conversation context. Resolve relative requests ("tomorrow at 9am", "in 3 hours", "next Monday") against the freshly fetched time, then echo the resolved local time AND the UTC timestamp back to the user for confirmation before creating the routine. If the resolved time is already in the past, ask the user to clarify rather than silently rolling forward.

## Workflow

### CREATE a new routine:

1. **Understand the goal** — Ask what they want the cloud agent to do. What repo(s)? What task? Remind them that the agent runs in the cloud — it won't have access to their local machine, local files, or local environment variables.
2. **Craft the prompt** — Help them write an effective agent prompt. Good prompts are:
   - Specific about what to do and what success looks like
   - Clear about which files/areas to focus on
   - Explicit about what actions to take (open PRs, commit, just analyze, etc.)
3. **Set the schedule** — Ask when and how often. The user's timezone is Asia/Calcutta. When they say a time (e.g., "every morning at 9am"), assume they mean their local time and convert to UTC for the cron expression. Always confirm the conversion: "9am Asia/Calcutta = Xam UTC." If they want a one-time run (e.g., "once at 3pm", "tomorrow morning", "remind me to check X later"), use `run_once_at` instead of `cron_expression` — same timezone conversion applies. **First re-check the current time with `date -u` via Bash** (the reference time above may be stale in a long conversation), resolve the relative phrase against that fresh value, and confirm the resulting absolute timestamp with the user.
4. **Choose the model** — Default to `claude-sonnet-5`. Tell the user which model you're defaulting to and ask if they want a different one.
5. **Validate connections** — Infer what services the agent will need from the user's description. For example, if they say "check Datadog and Slack me errors," the agent needs both Datadog and Slack MCP connectors. Cross-reference with the connectors list above. If any are missing, warn the user and link them to https://claude.ai/customize/connectors to connect first. Ask which git repos the cloud agent needs cloned into its environment.
6. **Review and confirm** — Show the full configuration before creating. Let them adjust.
7. **Create it** — Call `RemoteTrigger` with `action: "create"` and show the result. The response includes the routine ID. Always output a link at the end: `https://claude.ai/code/routines/{ROUTINE_ID}`

### UPDATE a routine:

1. List routines first so they can pick one
2. Ask what they want to change
3. Show current vs proposed value
4. Confirm and update

### LIST routines:

1. Fetch and display in a readable format
2. Show: name, schedule (human-readable), enabled/disabled, next run, repo(s)

### RUN NOW:

1. List routines if they haven't specified which one
2. Confirm which routine
3. Execute and confirm

## Important Notes

- These are CLOUD agents — they run in Anthropic's cloud, not on the user's machine. They cannot access local files, local services, or local environment variables.
- Always convert cron to human-readable when displaying
- When listing routines, `ended_reason: "run_once_fired"` means a one-shot already ran (shows as "Ran" in the web UI). The user can re-arm it by updating with a new `run_once_at`.
- Default to `enabled: true` unless user says otherwise
- Accept GitHub URLs in any format (https://github.com/org/repo, org/repo, etc.) and normalize to the full HTTPS URL (without .git suffix)
- The prompt is the most important part — spend time getting it right. The cloud agent starts with zero context, so the prompt must be self-contained.
- To delete a routine, direct users to https://claude.ai/code/routines

file.content:
# Exporting `Beacon-Submission-Ashish.pdf`

No new dependency goes into `package.json` for this — it's a one-off document export, not part of the scanned product. Use whichever of the two options below is already on your machine.

The PDF needs to stand on its own if a reviewer never opens the repo: page 1 must show the headline finding (with the example report screenshot) and the repo + Loom links, followed by all three essays. That means source order matters — `README.md` first (it already carries the headline, the screenshot, and the links table near the top), then the three essays.

## Option A — pandoc (preferred)

Install once if you don't have it:

```bash
brew install pandoc          # macOS
# or: apt-get install pandoc  # Linux
```

A PDF engine is also required — pandoc doesn't ship one. Easiest is `wkhtmltopdf` (no LaTeX install needed):

```bash
brew install wkhtmltopdf
```

Then, from the repo root, after `out/EXAMPLE/` and `docs/img/report.png` exist (post-Lane I / Ashish's real run):

```bash
pandoc README.md docs/part2-architecture.md docs/part2-defensibility.md docs/part3-discovery.md \
  --pdf-engine=wkhtmltopdf \
  --resource-path=.:docs:docs/img \
  --metadata title="Beacon Friction Scanner — Ashish Jain Kothari" \
  -o Beacon-Submission-Ashish.pdf
```

If you'd rather use a LaTeX engine (`--pdf-engine=xelatex` after `brew install --cask mactex-no-gui` or similar), swap the engine flag — the rest of the command is unchanged. `--resource-path` is what lets the `docs/img/report.png` reference in `README.md` resolve correctly when the source files sit in different directories.

Before exporting, either remove the `<!-- DRAFT: Ashish to edit voice -->` comment from the top of each essay (it renders as nothing in the PDF either way — HTML comments are stripped by pandoc — but removing it once the voice pass is done is the actual sign-off) or leave it if the PDF is still a draft round.

## Option B — VS Code, no terminal tools

1. Install the **"Markdown PDF"** extension (yzane.markdown-pdf) from the VS Code marketplace.
2. Open `README.md`, run **Markdown PDF: Export (pdf)** from the command palette, confirm the `docs/img/report.png` image renders (VS Code resolves relative paths from the file's own location, so this should work unmodified).
3. Repeat for each essay: `docs/part2-architecture.md`, `docs/part2-defensibility.md`, `docs/part3-discovery.md` — each exports as its own PDF.
4. Merge the four PDFs into one (`README.pdf` first, then the three essays in order) with any PDF tool you have — macOS Preview does this via **File → Print → the "Combine PDFs" step is actually easier via `Automator`'s "Combine PDF Pages" quick action, or `pdfunite` if you have poppler installed** (`brew install poppler && pdfunite README.pdf part2-architecture.pdf part2-defensibility.pdf part3-discovery.pdf Beacon-Submission-Ashish.pdf`).

Option A produces the single merged file directly and is less fiddly; Option B is here for a machine without pandoc/a PDF engine installed and no interest in installing one.

## Either way

Confirm before submitting:
- [ ] Page 1 shows the one-sentence description, the three headline numbers, and the repo + Loom links (all present near the top of `README.md`).
- [ ] The example report screenshot is visible, not a broken image icon.
- [ ] All three essays are present, in Part 2 (architecture) → Part 2 (defensibility) → Part 3 (discovery) order.
- [ ] `Beacon-Submission-Ashish.pdf` opens cleanly and isn't added to `package.json` as a dependency of anything.
